name: Tongue tie release

lead: Tongue-tie release cuts the frenulum under the tongue to improve tongue mobility. It is mostly used for infant breastfeeding problems, and sometimes for speech or mobility in older patients.
Online, some people link it to palate shape, jaw development and facial symmetry. These links are described as hypothesised, and no study was found testing release for appearance.

paras: A short incision or removal of the frenulum, using scissors, a scalpel or a laser, frees the tongue. Proponents of the symmetry idea say better tongue posture could influence the palate and jaw; this is described as speculative.

The procedure is typically quick with little reported pain. Experts debate overdiagnosis of minor restrictions, and reviews describe long-term benefits for feeding duration and speech as inconclusive.

lead: Tongue-tie release, also called frenotomy or frenectomy, is a minor surgical procedure that cuts or removes the lingual frenulum, the fold of tissue anchoring the tongue to the floor of the mouth, in people with ankyloglossia (tongue-tie).[1][2] It can be done with scissors, a scalpel or a laser, and a related procedure, frenuloplasty, adds suturing for more complex cases.[1][2]

The procedure is mainly used for infant feeding difficulties and, in some children and adults, for speech or mobility concerns. In looksmaxxing and related online discussion it is also raised as something that might influence tongue posture, palate shape, jaw development and facial symmetry. Wikipedia describes such links as possible and hypothesised and not established outcomes.[2]

Studies of frenotomy for breastfeeding report improvement in short-term outcomes, while systematic reviews describe the evidence as of moderate quality, with inconclusive long-term effects on breastfeeding duration or speech.[1][3] No study found tests release as a way to change facial symmetry or appearance.

paras: A frenectomy is the removal or incision of a frenulum. The main variants are lingual frenectomy, which releases the tongue attachment, and labial frenectomy, which treats lip attachments associated with gingival recession or a gap between the front teeth.[1] Frenotomy usually means a simple incision, often in infants, while frenuloplasty implies a reconstructive revision with sutures.[1]

As of 2025, Wikipedia notes that no generally accepted definition, classification or diagnostic criteria for tongue-tie exist, and severity ranges from mild mucosal bands to complete tethering of the tongue.[2] Assessment tools such as the Hazelbaker score are used in some settings.[1]

Meta-analyses estimate ankyloglossia in about 5% to 8% of infants, with rates varying with the diagnostic method, and higher in newborns presenting with breastfeeding difficulty.[1] Professionals disagree on how often it causes problems: some consider it rarely symptomatic and others link it to many issues.[2] Controversy about overdiagnosis of minor restrictions and the need for treatment without clear functional impairment is described.[1]

sections.h: Claims about facial and jaw development
paras: Wikipedia describes proposed, not established, associations: restricted tongue contact with the palate may prolong an infantile swallow pattern and could contribute to an open bite; forceful tongue thrusting may contribute to a prominent lower jaw; ankyloglossia is correlated with a narrow, V-shaped palate, tooth crowding, bruxism, jaw joint pain and mouth breathing; and a hypothesised fascial link may spread tension to the neck and jaw, described as speculative.[2] Whether release changes facial symmetry is not addressed in the sources reviewed.

A prospective cohort study of surgical tongue-tie and lip-tie release studied breastfeeding impairment before and after the procedure.[4] Reviews of frenotomy report short-term latch and nipple pain improvements in a majority of cases, with inconclusive evidence on breastfeeding duration and speech.[1] A systematic review of the diagnostic criteria and treatment of ankyloglossia examined 64 articles and the evidence regarding breastfeeding, speech and other issues.[3] For speech, several later systematic reviews and trials reported no difference in speech sound development between children who had surgery and those who did not.[2]

Frenectomy is typically quick and done under local anaesthesia, with dissolvable stitches, and most patients are reported to have little pain afterward.[2] Randomised comparisons of carbon dioxide laser and scalpel frenectomy have compared postoperative pain, eating and speech complications,[5] and other studies compare different laser types.[6] Non-surgical options include exercises from orofacial myology specialists, and many children are monitored, since the frenulum often recedes between roughly six months and six years of age.[2]

No studies found testing tongue-tie release for facial symmetry or appearance. Studies of frenotomy for infant feeding, speech and surgical technique exist,[3][4][5] and trials of frenectomy techniques are registered, including adults with a high frenum attachment (NCT06331325, n=46) and tongue mobility after frenectomy (NCT06856564, n=60).[7][8]

timeline.event: Messner and colleagues report breastfeeding difficulties in more mothers of infants with ankyloglossia than controls.[2]
Systematic review of diagnosis and treatment of ankyloglossia published.[3]
Prospective cohort study of tongue-tie and lip-tie release and breastfeeding published.[4]
